name: Mādhava
description: Madhava's 14th-century infinite series for π, and the Kerala correction terms that make it converge astonishingly fast.
aria: A twisting chain of light whose links are the terms of Madhava's series for pi
intro: In 14th-century Kerala, Mādhava wrote π as an infinite sum, then found how to correct the last term so a few dozen terms give eleven digits. Watch the series fold into π.

tutorial.t: π as a sum that never ends
tutorial.b: Mādhava, in 14th-century Kerala: π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + … forever. Here each term is a link in a chain: forward 1, back 1/3, forward 1/5.
tutorial.see: three links folded along a line. Forward, back, forward.

tutorial.b: Each new link overshoots the target, then undershoots, by less each time. The dashed line marks π/4, where it's heading. The catch: it's painfully slow. 1,000 terms give only 3 correct digits of π.
tutorial.see: the white tip of the chain bouncing either side of the dashed line.

tutorial.b: When you stop after n terms, you throw away an infinite tail. Mādhava found its size is predictable, so you add a correction to the last term. His sharpest one is (n²+1) / (n(4n²+5)).
tutorial.see: the gold dot: the corrected estimate, sitting almost exactly on π/4.

tutorial.b: Top left, the four rows show the same 25 terms with no correction and with each of Mādhava's three corrections. Without: off by 0.04. With the sharpest: off by about 10⁻¹⁰. Bright digits are correct.
tutorial.see: the digit counts on the right of each row.

tutorial.b: In the swing view each estimate is a ray, magnified so the error is visible. Rose rays are the plain sums: they swing wide. Gold rays have the correction: they land on π and stay. The magnification keeps growing, like zooming in forever.
tutorial.see: the rose fan wobbling while the gold ray sits still on the white π dot.

tutorial.b: Turn each link 120° from the last, not 180°, and the same series curls into a spiral. It's Mādhava's arctangent series evaluated around the unit circle. 180° is the one special angle where it folds flat into π.
tutorial.see: the spiral. Say 'twist 150' or 'twist 90' to try others, or 'play' to let it breathe.

sound:
Each term is a note. Every new term plucks a santoor string. The series alternates plus and minus, and so does the music: minus terms play three notes higher in the raag (from Sa that's Pa, × 3/2). That's why you hear a back-and-forth. Every 8 terms the base note climbs one step.

A singing bowl rings every time π gains a correct digit. With the correction on, the bowl rings often at first, then the digits run out of room on screen.

Every chamber plays in Raag Bhupali: five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as whole-number ratios of the home note Sa (138.6 Hz here): 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3. Simple ratios mean the sound waves line up every few cycles, so they never clash. That lets the math pick any note it likes and it still sounds like music. Underneath, a tanpura drone holds Sa and Pa, and a bansuri improvises in the same raag. The santoor and the singing bowl are the ones the math plays.

faq.a: Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma (c. 1340–1425), founder of the Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics. His results survive through Nīlakaṇṭha's Tantrasaṅgraha and Jyeṣṭhadeva's Yuktibhāṣā.
Europe calls it the Gregory–Leibniz series, from the 1670s, roughly 250 years after Mādhava.
Stop after n terms and add (−1)ⁿ·F(n) to the sum. The Yuktibhāṣā gives F = 1/(4n), then n/(4n²+1), then (n²+1)/(n(4n²+5)). Each one is far sharper than the last.
Plain series: 1,000 terms for 3 digits. With the sharpest correction, 25 terms give about 10 digits.
Each link turns by an angle θ from the last. The chain's end is Σ zᵏ/(2k+1) with z = e^{iθ}. At 180°, z = −1 and it folds onto Mādhava's series for π/4.
Each estimate of π is a ray, its error magnified until the plain sums swing about ±60°. Rose: plain sums. Gold: with the correction, landing on π.
Bhupali uses five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as the ratios 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2 and 5/3. It has no half-steps, so any note the math picks sounds consonant against the drone.

Sa is 138.6 Hz. Every other note is Sa times a whole-number ratio (9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3) or that times a power of 2 for higher octaves. Which note plays is chosen by a number in the scene. Open 'why this sound' to watch it live.
The haze behind the math is a kaleidoscope shader. Its symmetry follows the chamber's math, but it's decoration. Say 'trip 0' to switch it off and see only the math.
Isha Maini, a data science student at Emory. Each chamber's math is written and tested in Python and JavaScript before it's drawn.
